latin.438: §. VII. Protruso hac ratione in publicam lucem Transsubstantiationis monstro horrendo (cui lumen tamen ademtum adhuc omne erat, quòd post aliquod demum temporis spatium, nomine tandem suo proprio se exornatum vidit) Decretis summorum Paparum, ex ipsa etiam Romana Petri sede pronuntiantium, in thronum firmiter satis collocatum stabilitumque est.
latin.439: Postquam nempe de vero Conversionis in Eucharistia Modo, à Scholasticis & horum principe Petro Lombardo lib. 4. dist. 11. pag. m. 311. 312. 313. subtiliter æquè atque acriter disputatum esset.
latin.440: Nam tum, Seculo nempe XII. medio, per Petrum Blesensem Epistola 140, juxta Caveum p. 471, juxta alios per Stephanum Æduensem vel Augustodunensem Episcopum, de Sacramento Altaris in Bibliotheca Patrum (cujus tamen Autoris & ætas & scripta valdè incerta sunt) Transsubstantiationis nomen adinventum.
latin.441: Et Seculo seq. XIII. anno 1215. ab Innocentio III. Papa, in Lateranensi Concilio suo canonizatum est.
latin.442: Auctor tantæ Canonizationis se sermonibus suis, ceu sorex voce, prodit, hunc in modum suos allocutus: Mihi, inquit, dicitur in Propheta: Constitui te super gentes & regna &c. &c. Has Innocentii allocutiones omnes cum laudatissimus Dunelmensis pag. 149. recensuisset, subjicit pag. 150: Hæc ille Christi jam factus, non Vicarius modo, sed etiam Rivalis, quæ nunc commemoro, ut videamus qualis fuerit rerum conditio & Latinæ Ecclesiæ facies, quando Transsubstantiatio pro fidei articulo ab Innocentio Papa proposita est & obtrusa.
latin.443: Canon Canonizationis in Extravag. de Fide & summ. Trinit. Firmiter credimus &c. his verbis legitur: Una verò est fidelium universalis Ecclesia, extra quam nullus omnino salvatur. In qua idem ipse sacerdos & sacrificium Jesus Christus; hujus corpus & sanguis in Sacramento Altaris sub speciebus panis & vini veraciter continentur: TRANSSUBSTANTIATIS pane in corpus & vino in sanguinem, potestate divina, ut ad perficiendum mysterium unitatis accipiamus ipsi de suo, quod ipse accepit de nostro. Et hoc utique Sacramentum nemo potest conficere, nisi Sacerdos fuerit ritè ordinatus secundum claves Ecclesiæ, quas ipse concessit Apostolis & eorum successoribus Jesus Christus. Vide etiam Sagittar. retrò citatum, p. 495. in fin.

pass_a.438: §. VII. The horrible monster of Transsubstantiation having by this means been thrust forth into public light (to which nonetheless all light was still taken away, because only after some space of time at last it saw itself adorned with its own proper name) was by Decrees of the highest Popes, pronouncing even from the Roman See of Peter itself, placed and established firmly enough upon a throne.
pass_a.439: Namely after the true Mode of Conversion in the Eucharist had been disputed by the Scholastics and their prince Peter Lombard, book 4 distinction 11 pp. 311–313, as subtly as sharply.
pass_a.440: For then, namely in the middle of the twelfth Century, through Peter of Blois Epistle 140, according to Cave p. 471, according to others through Stephen Bishop of Autun (Æduensis / Augustodunensis), On the Sacrament of the Altar in the Bibliotheca Patrum (whose author’s age and writings are nonetheless very uncertain), the name of Transsubstantiation was invented.
pass_a.441: And in the following thirteenth Century, in the year 1215, it was canonized by Pope Innocent III in his Lateran Council.
pass_a.442: The author of so great a Canonization betrays himself by his sermons, as a shrew by its voice, addressing his own in this manner: To me, he says, it is said in the Prophet: I have set you over nations and kingdoms &c. When the most praiseworthy Dunelm had reviewed all these allocutions of Innocent at p. 149, he adds at p. 150: These things that one, already made not only Vicar but even Rival of Christ, I now commemorate, that we may see what the condition of affairs and the face of the Latin Church was when Transsubstantiation was proposed and thrust by Pope Innocent as an article of faith.
pass_a.443: The Canon of Canonization in the Extravagantes De Fide & summa Trinitate, Firmiter credimus &c., is read in these words: There is one universal Church of the faithful, outside which no one at all is saved. In which Jesus Christ Himself is both priest and sacrifice; His body and blood are truly contained in the Sacrament of the Altar under the species of bread and wine: the bread having been TRANSUBSTANTIATED into body and the wine into blood by divine power, that to perfect the mystery of unity we ourselves may receive of His what He received of ours. And this Sacrament indeed no one can confect unless he be a Priest duly ordained according to the keys of the Church, which Jesus Christ Himself granted to the Apostles and their successors. See also Sagittarius cited above, p. 495 at the end.

438: §.VII: by this path the horrible Transsubstantiation-monster is thrust into public light — yet still without its proper name.
Papal decrees from Peter’s Roman seat plant it firmly enough on a throne.
439: That seating follows Scholastic dispute on the true Conversion-mode in the Eucharist.
Lombard (bk. 4 dist. 11 pp. 311–313) leads — subtle and sharp alike.
440: Mid-twelfth century: the name Transsubstantiation is invented.
Cave points to Peter of Blois Ep. 140; others to Stephen of Autun On the Sacrament of the Altar (Bibliotheca Patrum — author and date very uncertain).
441: Next century, 1215: Pope Innocent III canonizes that name in his Lateran Council.
So the invented term Transsubstantiatio becomes a canon of the faith under Lateran IV.
442: Innocent betrays the author of the canonization in his own sermons — ‘To me it is said in the Prophet: I have set you over nations and kingdoms…’ (as a shrew by its voice).
Dunelm (pp. 149–150): commemorate this already Rival of Christ, not mere Vicar, to see the Latin Church’s face when Transsubstantiation was thrust as an article of faith.
443: Firmiter (Extravag. De Fide & summa Trinitate): one universal Church; Christ’s body and blood truly under bread and wine species.
Key clause: bread TRANSUBSTANTIATED into body and wine into blood by divine power — only a duly ordained priest may confect (Sagittarius p. 495).
Stop before §.VIII (still on the Scholastic anvil after canonization).
